passage: Sit, Pooja. You asked why your Vasudha Masi goes quiet in meetings even now. When I was twenty-four, my first boss at the insurance office was a Mr Kulkarni. Each morning, before I opened my mouth, I read his face: a loosened tie meant a good day; a file slammed on the desk meant say nothing. I had ideas, good ones, about the claims backlog. I wrote them in my diary and never said them aloud. When he asked, "Any objections?" I'd smile and say, "It's perfect, sir." Slowly I stopped even noticing my own opinions. I remember walking home feeling small, as if I'd shrunk an inch by evening. That habit stayed long after he retired. So when your manager asks what you think, tell her. Practise while it's cheap.

qa.q: What did a loosened tie mean to Vasudha?
qa.a: A loosened tie meant a good day.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel walking home in the evenings?
qa.a: Vasudha felt small, as if she'd shrunk an inch by evening, after hiding her views all day 😔

qa.q: What choice does Vasudha want Pooja to make that she did not?
qa.a: Vasudha wants Pooja to answer honestly when the manager asks for an opinion, practising while it's cheap, instead of learning to go quiet.

qa.q: What would change if Mr Kulkarni had welcomed objections?
qa.a: Vasudha's ideas on the claims backlog might have been heard, and she might not have carried the habit of silence for years.

grounding: An aunt recalls learning to read a powerful boss's moods, hide her views and shrink, as a young insurance employee.

passage: The slab had to be poured before the rain, and Hemant sir was in one of his moods. Raghav, twenty-four and eight months into the job, could tell from the way his boss chewed the pen cap: a fast chew meant anyone who spoke would be shouted at in front of the labourers. Raghav had spotted a sagging prop under the east corner of the shuttering. He rehearsed the sentence three times in his head. "Sir, the east corner..." Hemant turned. "What? Speak or move." "Nothing, sir. All ready." Raghav went and quietly wedged in an extra prop himself, hands shaking, as the first drops fell. The slab held. Nobody knew. That night on the bus Raghav realised he hadn't said one full sentence of his own all week.

qa.q: What did a fast chew on the pen cap mean?
qa.a: A fast chew meant anyone who spoke would be shouted at in front of the labourers.

qa.q: Why did Raghav say "Nothing, sir. All ready."?
qa.a: Raghav was afraid of being shouted at in front of the labourers, so fear of Hemant's mood swallowed the warning about the sagging prop.

qa.q: What went wrong at the key moment, and what could Raghav try next time?
qa.a: Raghav's warning died under Hemant's impatience; next time Raghav could lead with the plain fact, "The east corner prop is sagging," or tell another engineer so safety doesn't rest on one silent fix.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant asked the team for problems before a pour?
qa.a: Raghav could raise a sagging prop openly, and the site would not depend on a scared junior quietly fixing it in the rain.

grounding: Shows a junior engineer under deadline and rain reading a boss's moods and swallowing a warning, feeling he has lost his own voice.

passage: Every morning at the Andheri office, Kashish checked two things before logging in: the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat. A cheerful "Morning, team!" meant she could ask for the leave she needed. A bare "Status?" meant keep your head down. Six months in, she had learned to rewrite her reports so the bad numbers sat at the bottom, softened. In meetings she waited to see which way Sachin leaned, then agreed. When he called her idea for the client deck "cute", she laughed along and deleted the slide. At home her flatmate asked what she thought about the new project. Kashish opened her mouth and found she didn't know anymore; she only knew what Sachin thought.

qa.q: What two things did Kashish check every morning before logging in?
qa.a: Kashish checked the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat.

qa.q: What does Kashish's blank moment with her flatmate show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows Kashish has muted her own voice so long that she feels unsure of her own opinion and only knows Sachin's.

qa.q: What small choice could help Kashish get her own view back?
qa.a: Kashish could write down her own opinion before each meeting and keep one honest line about the bad numbers near the top of her reports.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Kashish, compared with what she actually thinks?
qa.a: Sachin probably sees an agreeable employee with no objections, not knowing her real ideas and doubts are hidden to please him.

grounding: Illustrates a junior employee watching a manager's moods, hiding her views and losing touch with her own opinions.

passage: "Naveen, you've been in front of that mirror for ten minutes." Suraj leaned on the bathroom door. "I'm practising. 'Sir, I have a small suggestion.' No. 'Sir, if you have a moment.' No." "For what?" "The client proposal. My numbers are better than his." "So tell him." Naveen laughed without humour. "You don't know Bhatia sir. If he comes in whistling, you can speak. If he takes his glasses off, you say, 'Yes sir, very good sir.'" "And today?" "Glasses off." "So you said nothing." "I said his plan was excellent." Suraj was quiet. "Bhaiya, at college you argued with the dean." "That was college." Naveen rinsed his face. "Now I just watch his glasses." "You've gone smaller," Suraj said. "Since you joined." Naveen looked at himself in the mirror and didn't answer.

qa.q: What does Bhatia sir do when Naveen should say only 'Yes sir'?
qa.a: He takes his glasses off.

qa.q: What does Naveen's rehearsing in the mirror suggest about how he feels at work?
qa.a: It suggests he feels nervous and watchful, so unsure of his boss's mood that he has to practise even a small suggestion.

qa.q: What small step could Naveen take with his better numbers?
qa.a: He could send the numbers in a short written note, so his idea is on record even on a 'glasses off' day.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the change in his older brother?
qa.a: Suraj sees that Naveen, who once argued with the dean, has become quieter and smaller since joining this job.

grounding: A young employee learns to read his boss's moods and say only what pleases, and his brother sees him shrinking.

passage: I'm Yamini. At twenty-four I got my first cook's job in Vaibhav Chef's restaurant kitchen, and I learned to read him before I learned his recipes. If he tied his apron twice round, the day was fine. If he came in with it hanging loose, nobody spoke unless spoken to. I had ideas. I thought the dal could use less cream, and I knew the order system wasted food. I said none of it. On good days he called me beti. When he asked, "Any problems?" I said, "No, Chef." I tasted my own cooking less and his mood more. After a year, a new girl asked me what I thought of the menu, and I opened my mouth and realised I didn't know. I'd been so busy watching the apron that I had stopped having opinions. I felt about half my size.

qa.q: What did it mean when Vaibhav Chef tied his apron twice round?
qa.a: It meant the day was fine.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel after a year in that kitchen, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt small and lost, since she could not answer the new girl's question and felt about half her size.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and what could she do next?
qa.a: Being asked her opinion and finding she had none showed her how much she had hidden; she could start by writing down one idea a week and sharing it on a good day.

qa.q: How might the new girl see Yamini when she cannot answer?
qa.a: The new girl might be surprised, expecting a cook with a year's experience to have clear views on the menu.

grounding: A young cook learns to read a powerful chef's moods and hide her views, and slowly feels smaller.
